perspective:
From Harold Padilla’s perspective, he has access to the following information:

- He is a project manager. He believes his project team is not performing well and seems unmotivated, and this is affecting progress. He feels frustrated, anxious, and at his wit’s end.
- He has a friend/advisor, Arthur Begum, whom he trusts for advice. Harold arranged a coffee-shop meeting with Arthur to discuss the team problem.
- Harold told Arthur about the unmotivated team and heard Arthur advise him to understand what drives each team member individually, have one-on-one conversations, and make people feel valued and understood.
- After speaking with Arthur, Harold felt hopeful and relieved. He decided to implement Arthur’s suggestion.
- Harold told his team they would have quick one-on-one chats to understand what motivates each of them. He heard Team Member 1 say that could be helpful and Team Member 2 say they were open to it. Harold said he would schedule time with each of them.
- Later, Harold noticed the team still was not responding well. He felt disappointed and worried about the project’s future, and he returned to Arthur for advice.
- Harold heard Arthur suggest there might be deeper issues: personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors. Arthur advised him to dig deeper.
- Harold then held one-on-one meetings with team members to investigate concerns. He heard Team Member 1 say there was tension between a few team members affecting work. He heard Team Member 2 say they felt overwhelmed by the workload and stressed. Harold said he would look into resolving conflicts and see if tasks could be redistributed, and he told them their well-being was important to him.
- After that, Harold felt optimistic and empowered. He believed addressing individual concerns would improve team performance.
- Harold told the team he would create a more supportive and open environment by implementing regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. He heard Team Member 1 and Team Member 2 respond positively.
- Harold wants the project to succeed and believes team input and well-being are crucial to that success.

He does **not** have access to any private thoughts or hidden information beyond what he personally felt, observed, heard, said, or did in these interactions.
